blocks.text: Urinary stones are hard, crystalline mineral materials that-stick together to form small "pebbles" within the kidney or urinary tract. They may stay in kidneys or travel out of the body through the urinary tract.

70% of kidney stone patients have stones of calcium oxalate. These stones are formed due to hypercalciuria (high calcium in urine) and hyperoxaluria (increased level of oxalate level in urine). 10% of patients may have stones of uric acid. Hyperuricemia (increased amount of uric acid in blood) is the cause of such stones. High concentration of cysteine and phosphates in urine also cause kidney stones. Continuous dehydration in the body increases the chances of kidney stone formation. Treatment of kidney stones usually involves lithotripsy i.e., breaking of stones. There are two methods of lithotripsy.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The stones meant here are cystine stones. Cystine (two cysteine molecules joined together) is poorly soluble and crystallises in urine; the book prints 'cysteine'.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Doctors diagnose the nature of kidney stone by studying the urine test of patient. When urine is acidic, the stone is of calcium oxalate. When the urine is alkaline, the stone is of calcium phosphate. When urine is persistently acidic, the stone is of uric acid type.

In Extracorporeal Shockwave Lithotripsy (ECSWL), an instrument called lithotripter generates shockwaves from outside the patient's body. These shockwaves break the stone into small pieces. Most of pieces then pass out through urine.

blocks.alt: A patient sits against a support while a lithotripter outside the body sends shockwaves towards the kidney. Two enlarged circles show the kidney: in the first, shockwaves reach a stone in the renal pelvis; in the second, the stone has broken into smaller pieces.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.5: Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.5).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Lithotripter, Shockwaves (at the body and in the first enlargement), Stones, Smaller pieces of stones.

blocks.text: In case of larger stones, Percutaneous Nephrolithotripsy (PNL) is used. In this technique, a tube is inserted from the patient's back into the kidney. A small camera called nephroscope is inserted through the tube to visualize the stone. Ultrasound equipment is then inserted to break the stone. The stone pieces can be grasped with special equipment and pulled out from the kidney.

blocks.alt: A section through the back with a kidney. A tube passes from outside through the skin into the renal pelvis; a stone lies where the ureter begins. A flexible line joins the tube to a nephroscope outside the body.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.6: Percutaneous Nephrolithotripsy (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.6).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Renal pelvis, Stone, Skin, Tube, Nephroscope.
